messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always taken pride in his decades-long service in the Coast Guard, but it was a single incident involving toxic chemical exposure that changed everything. He remembered the day vividly - the smell of the chemicals, the sound of his colleagues' panicked voices, and the feeling of helplessness as he watched the scene unfold. Even now, when Kofi closes his eyes, the memory replays like a film in his mind, each frame seared into his brain with photographic precision. As time passed, Kofi began to notice that unusual silence made him feel on edge. He would find himself scanning the room, waiting for something to happen, even in the safety of his own home. His wife, Akua, would try to reassure him, but Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. This sense of threat was constantly fueled by memories of the chemical exposure, which seemed to replay on a loop in his mind. When these memories surfaced, Kofi felt overwhelmed by emotion, and he would have to stop whatever he was doing to collect himself. Kofi had come to believe that he couldn't deal with even the slightest upset. He thought that if he allowed himself to think about the event, he wouldn't be able to handle it, and this fear of being overwhelmed led him to avoid thinking about it altogether. However, this avoidance only seemed to reinforce his conviction that the world was a dangerous place, and that he needed to be constantly on guard. This sense of threat, in turn, made Kofi more prone to strong physical reactions when something reminded him of the stressful experience. As Kofi's symptoms worsened, he found it increasingly difficult to navigate his daily routine. He would become easily startled by sudden noises, and even the sight of certain chemicals or equipment would trigger a strong reaction. His wife began to notice the changes in him, and she encouraged him to seek help. But Kofi was hesitant, convinced that he couldn't cope with the emotions that therapy might stir up. Despite his reservations, Kofi's worsening symptoms eventually led him to seek professional help. He is now struggling to come to terms with the fact that his traumatic experience has left an indelible mark on his life. As he begins this new chapter, Kofi is most afraid of losing control and being overwhelmed by his emotions. But he also hopes that therapy will help him find a way to quiet the constant threat alerts in his mind, and learn to navigate the world with a sense of safety and security once again.
